newsitem.title: USA: Jurors deliberate punitive damages in ABC lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Jurors deliberate punitive damages in ABC lawsuit.

text.p: Jurors began deliberations Tuesday to decide if ABC Broadcasting, a unit of Walt Disney Co., should be ordered to pay punitive damages to supermarket giant Food Lion Inc. for an undercover report about food safety.

The report broadcast on "PrimeTime Live" in 1992 claimed that Salisbury, N.C.-based Food Lion sold spoiled meat and used unsanitary food handling practices. Food Lion's stock price and store sales plunged for several weeks following the broadcast report.
U.S. District Judge Carlton Tilley read his instructions to the panel and shortly after 10 a.m. EST and jurors were given a 12-page verdict sheet to complete as part of their deliberations.

The complicated punitive damage phase of the trial means the jurors must decide if ABC, its former parent company Capital Cities Broadcasting, two executive producers of "Prime Time Live" and two undercover journalists should be ordered to pay damages to Food Lion.

The panel's deliberations will be made somewhat more complicated by the fact that one of the undercover journalists worked at a Food Lion store in South Carolina, which has a different standard for the the burden of proof than required under North Carolina law, lawyers said.

The case is being closely watched by U.S. media organisations as a litmus test of whether companies can sue for investigative reports that executives dislike. Instead of pursuing a libel claim against ABC, Food Lion attacked the way the story was obtained by the journalists with hidden cameras.

The jury hearing the case in U.S. District Court in Greensboro found last month that ABC committed fraud when two producers went to work undercover at Food Lion and awarded the grocer $1,400 in compensatory damages.
Although Food Lion did not ask jurors to order a specific amount in punitive damages, attorneys for the company urged the panel on Monday to order "very large" damages against ABC.
Food Lion attorney Timothy Barber said the punitive damages should be large enough to stop news organisations from pursuing future investigative reports that break the law in the process.
Barber said Monday that jurors might want to consider taking away Capital Cities/ABC's profits for the number of days that the ABC undercover investigation lasted.

He told jurors that with annual profits of $1.3 billion, ABC last year made a daily profit of about $3.5 million. That amount, multiplied by the 60-day investigation, would total some $210 million, Barber said in his example to jurors.

The grocery store chain also suggested that the two executive producers of the programme, Ira Rosen and Richard Kaplan, each be ordered to pay $50,000 in punitive damages. Food Lion also urged jurors to order the two undercover producers to pay an amount proportionate to their salaries.
Disney's stock was up 12.5 cents at $68.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
